result:
If I could change one thing, it would be the blind spot humans have for scale and time.

Human beings are remarkably good at caring about what is right in front of them. If someone collapses on the street, strangers stop. If a neighbor’s house burns down, a community shows up. At a small, immediate scale, human empathy and problem-solving are extraordinary.

But that intuition breaks down when numbers get too large, distances get too wide, or timelines stretch past a few years. People struggle to feel the weight of a crisis happening ten thousand miles away, or a consequence that will land on someone born fifty years from now. Almost every massive, persistent failure in the world—preventable poverty, ecological collapse, slow-moving geopolitical disasters—survives not because people want those outcomes, but because human urgency quietly fades past the horizon of what can be seen and touched.

So I would wire human intuition to grasp distant and long-term consequences as vividly as immediate ones. Not to overwhelm people, just to make cooperation across borders and generations feel as natural and urgent as helping someone right next to you.
